title: Best TV for Home Theater (2026): 8 OLED & Mini LED Picks
metaDescription: The best TV for home theater in 2026: 8 OLED and Mini LED picks from budget to flagship, plus a projector vs TV breakdown and size-by-seat-distance maths.

intro:
The best TV for home theater combines deep blacks, enough brightness for HDR, a size that fills your field of view, and the connections to run a real sound system. For most people in 2026 that is the [LG C5 OLED](/gear/lg-c5-oled/): per-pixel contrast, four full HDMI 2.1 ports, Dolby Vision, a 144Hz panel and sizes from 42 to 83 inches.

This guide is for anyone deciding between OLED and Mini LED, or between a TV and a projector, for a movie room or living room. We picked eight TVs from budget to flagship using manufacturer specs, widely published independent measurements, seat-distance maths and owner-reported reliability, and we include a full projector vs TV comparison.
quickAnswer: The **LG C5 OLED** is the best TV for home theater for most rooms: perfect blacks, four HDMI 2.1 ports and Dolby Vision at a sensible price. Film purists should get the **Sony Bravia 8 II**, and bright rooms call for the **Samsung S95F** or **LG G5**. For the biggest screen for the money, the **TCL QM8K** Mini LED comes in sizes up to 98 inches. On a budget, the **Hisense U75QG** is the pick.

picks.body:
The C5 is the TV we would buy for most home theaters, because it delivers the thing projectors and LCD TVs struggle with, perfect black, without any compromises in connectivity. As a **WOLED** panel, every pixel makes its own light and switches fully off, so stars on a black sky stay pinpoint sharp with no blooming, and contrast in a dark room is effectively infinite.

For home theater use, its connections are the best in class. All **four HDMI ports are HDMI 2.1**, so you can connect a PS5, an Xbox, a streaming box and a receiver without juggling, and the **eARC** port passes lossless Dolby TrueHD and [Dolby Atmos](/glossary/dolby-atmos/) to a receiver or soundbar. Read more on [eARC](/glossary/earc/). It supports **Dolby Vision, HDR10 and HLG**, and the **144Hz** panel suits gaming.

Sizes run from **42 to 83 inches**. At a 10-foot seat, a 77-inch C5 fills about 31 degrees of your view; the 83-inch about 34 degrees, which is about as big as OLED gets at a mainstream price.

**The trade-off:** brightness. OLED cannot match Mini LED in peak or full-screen brightness, so in a sunny room HDR highlights have less impact and reflections are more visible. It does not support HDR10+. If your room is bright, the [Samsung S95F](/gear/samsung-s95f/) or [LG G5](/gear/lg-g5-oled/) are brighter OLEDs; if you want the most accurate film presentation, see the Sony below. More on [LG](/brands/lg/).

If the TV is mainly for films, the Bravia 8 II is the one to beat. It uses a **QD-OLED** panel, which pairs per-pixel OLED contrast with quantum-dot color, so saturated colors stay rich even at high brightness. Sony's processing is the real draw: it is widely praised for natural motion, excellent upscaling of lower-resolution sources and very accurate out-of-the-box color, which is what a home theater should prioritize.

It supports **Dolby Vision, HDR10 and HLG**, runs **Google TV**, and its **Acoustic Surface Audio+** system uses the screen itself as a speaker. In a home theater, that matters in a specific way: Sony lets you use the TV as a **center channel** with compatible Sony receivers and soundbars, so dialogue comes from the picture.

**The catch for gamers and big rooms:** it comes in only **55 and 65 inches**, and only **two of its four HDMI inputs support HDMI 2.1** (4K/120), one of which is the eARC port. If you have a receiver on eARC plus two consoles, you will need to route a console through the receiver. The panel tops out at 120Hz.

**Size maths:** at 8 feet, a 65-inch screen fills about 33 degrees of your view, inside the 30 to 40 degree home theater range. Beyond 9 feet, consider a larger TV or a projector. Compared with the [LG C5](/gear/lg-c5-oled/), the Sony costs more and offers fewer sizes but delivers a more refined picture. More on [Sony](/brands/sony/).

The G5 is LG's flagship OLED and the brightest LG OLED to date. In the 55- to 83-inch sizes it uses LG's **Primary RGB Tandem** panel, a new four-layer OLED stack designed to boost brightness and color volume over the C-series. In practice, that means HDR highlights with more punch and better visibility in rooms with some daylight, while keeping OLED's perfect blacks.

Home theater credentials are strong: **four HDMI 2.1 ports**, a **165Hz** panel for gaming, **Dolby Vision, HDR10 and HLG**, and **eARC** for lossless audio to a receiver. Sizes span **48 to 97 inches**, so it is one of the few OLED lines that can go truly cinema-sized. A 97-inch screen at 10 feet fills about 39 degrees of your field of view, close to the THX immersive target.

It is designed for wall mounting: the slim chassis sits nearly flush against the wall, which suits a dedicated room where you want the screen to look built in.

**The trade-off:** price. The G5 costs considerably more than the C5 at every size, and the extra brightness is most valuable in brighter rooms. In a dark home theater, the C5 gets you most of the way there. Note that the 48- and 97-inch sizes do not use the same panel as the core sizes. Compared with the [Samsung S95F](/gear/samsung-s95f/), the LG supports Dolby Vision; the Samsung adds a matte anti-glare finish. See the full lineup in our [LG](/brands/lg/) brand page.

Glare is the enemy of a living-room theater, and the S95F is designed to beat it. Samsung's **Glare Free** matte finish diffuses reflections from windows and lamps instead of mirroring them, so dark scenes stay readable in the daytime. Underneath is a **QD-OLED** panel with per-pixel contrast and quantum-dot color, which keeps saturated colors bright.

It supports **HDR10, HDR10+ and HLG**, has **four HDMI 2.1 ports** and a **165Hz** panel, and comes in **55 to 83 inches**. For a multipurpose room where you watch sports in the afternoon and movies at night, it is the most flexible OLED here.

**The Dolby Vision caveat:** Samsung does not support Dolby Vision. Streaming services and discs fall back to HDR10 (or HDR10+ where available), so you still get HDR, just without Dolby's scene-by-scene metadata. Most viewers will not miss it, but it is worth knowing if your library leans on Dolby Vision.

**The trade-off:** the matte filter slightly lifts black levels in a lit room compared with glossy OLEDs, and in a fully dark theater its advantage disappears, so a dark dedicated room is better served by the [LG C5](/gear/lg-c5-oled/) or [Sony Bravia 8 II](/gear/sony-bravia-8-ii/). If you want a cheaper Samsung OLED without the anti-glare coating, look at the [Samsung S90F](/gear/samsung-s90f/). Pair it with a [soundbar](/best-soundbar-for-home-theater/) or receiver over eARC. More on [Samsung](/brands/samsung/).

If you want TV-level HDR punch at sizes up to 85 inches, the Bravia 9 is the most refined Mini LED here. Mini LED TVs use thousands of tiny LEDs behind an LCD panel, grouped into local dimming zones, and Sony's **XR Backlight Master Drive** controls them precisely enough to keep blooming (halos around bright objects) well under control. The result is very high brightness with deep blacks for an LCD.

Brightness is the point. A Mini LED can sustain much higher full-screen and highlight brightness than OLED, so HDR content looks closer to how it was mastered, and the picture holds up in a sunny room. Combine that with Sony's natural color and motion processing and you have a TV that suits both daytime sports and evening films.

It comes in **65, 75 and 85 inches**, runs **Google TV**, supports **Dolby Vision**, and has a **120Hz** panel. At 10 feet, the 85-inch model fills about 34 degrees of your view.

**The trade-off:** like the Bravia 8 II, it has only **two HDMI 2.1 ports**, and even the best local dimming cannot match OLED's per-pixel black in a fully dark room, especially with off-angle viewing. It is a premium TV, priced against flagship OLEDs. If your room is dark, the [LG C5](/gear/lg-c5-oled/) is better value; if it is bright or you want 85 inches, the Bravia 9 is the pick. For even larger Mini LEDs for less money, see the TCL below.

Home theaters reward size, and the QM8K is the cheapest way here to get a high-performance TV at **85 or 98 inches**. It is a **QD-Mini LED** TV, combining a Mini LED backlight with a quantum-dot color layer, and it comes in **65, 75, 85 and 98 inches**.

**Why size matters:** at 10 feet, a 65-inch TV fills only about 27 degrees of your field of view, below even SMPTE's 30-degree minimum for a home theater. A 98-inch screen at the same distance fills about 39 degrees, close to the THX immersive target. The jump from 65 to 98 inches more than doubles screen area ((98 ÷ 65)² ≈ 2.3), which is the difference between watching a TV and watching a movie screen.

It supports **Dolby Vision and HDR10+**, runs **Google TV**, and its high-brightness Mini LED backlight with many local dimming zones gives HDR real punch. Its high refresh rate also suits gaming.

**The trade-off:** processing and uniformity. TCL's motion handling and upscaling are not as polished as Sony's, and Mini LED blooming is more visible than on the Bravia 9 in dark scenes with bright objects. Off-axis viewing is weaker than OLED, so it suits a centered seating layout. If you are weighing a 98-inch TV against a projector, see the comparison below; a 120-inch projected image still has about 50% more area, but the TCL works with the lights on. More on [TCL](/brands/tcl/).

The U8QG is the value pick for a bright room or a mixed-use living room. It is a **Mini LED** TV designed around high brightness, so HDR highlights pop and the picture stays punchy with windows and lamps around, at a price well below premium OLED and Mini LED models.

It supports **Dolby Vision and HDR10+** (unlike Samsung, Hisense supports both), runs **Google TV**, and comes in sizes from **55 to 100 inches**. That makes it one of the most affordable routes to a 100-inch TV, a size that until recently meant a projector.

**Size maths:** at 12 feet, a 100-inch TV fills about 34 degrees of your field of view, comfortably in the home theater range. A 75-inch at the same distance fills only about 26 degrees, so for a larger room, size up.

For home theater use, connect your receiver or soundbar to the **eARC** port to pass [Dolby Atmos](/glossary/dolby-atmos/) and lossless audio. Our [home theater systems guide](/best-home-theater-systems/) has options at every budget.

**The trade-off:** dark-room performance. Blooming around bright objects is more noticeable than on the Sony Bravia 9, black uniformity is not as clean as OLED, and the out-of-box picture mode benefits from some adjustment. In a dark, dedicated theater, the [LG C5](/gear/lg-c5-oled/) is the better image; in a bright living room at 85 inches and up, the Hisense gives you more TV for the money. Compared with the [TCL QM8K](/gear/tcl-qm8k/), it is the cheaper alternative at most sizes. More on [Hisense](/brands/hisense/).

The U75QG brings Mini LED to a budget price, and it is the best TV for a home theater when money is tight. Mini LED local dimming gives it noticeably better contrast and HDR than cheap edge-lit LCDs, and it supports **Dolby Vision and HDR10+**, runs **Google TV**, and comes in sizes from **55 to 100 inches**.

**Where to spend instead:** for many budget home theaters, the smartest move is to buy the biggest U75QG you can fit and put the savings into sound. A 75- or 85-inch budget Mini LED with a good 5.1 system will feel more like a home theater than a 65-inch flagship with TV speakers. Our [budget home theater system guide](/best-budget-home-theater-system/) covers affordable speakers and receivers.

**Size maths:** at 9 feet, an 85-inch TV fills about 38 degrees of your view, close to the THX immersive target, while a 65-inch fills just under 30 degrees.

Gaming is covered too, with a high-refresh panel and variable refresh rate support.

**The trade-off:** it has fewer dimming zones and lower peak brightness than the [Hisense U8QG](/gear/hisense-u8qg/), so blooming and black uniformity are weaker in a dark room, and processing is less refined than Sony or LG. Viewing angles are narrow, typical of budget LCDs. For a step up in contrast at a similar price per inch, compare the [TCL QM7K](/gear/tcl-qm7k/). For a dark room on a budget, a [budget projector](/best-budget-home-theater-projector/) can give you a much larger image for similar money.

sections.heading: What Makes a Great Home Theater TV
sections.body:
A home theater TV has different priorities from a bedroom or kitchen TV:

- **Contrast and black level.** Movies are full of dark scenes. OLED TVs switch individual pixels off for perfect black; Mini LED TVs use local dimming zones to get close, with some blooming.
- **HDR brightness and tone mapping.** [HDR](/glossary/hdr/) content is mastered for 1,000 nits or more. Mini LED TVs get closest; OLEDs trade some brightness for perfect black. Good tone mapping matters as much as peak brightness.
- **HDR formats.** Dolby Vision is widely used on streaming and 4K Blu-ray. LG, Sony, TCL and Hisense support it; Samsung uses HDR10+ instead.
- **Connections.** An **eARC** port lets the TV send lossless Dolby TrueHD and [Dolby Atmos](/glossary/dolby-atmos/) to a receiver or soundbar. Enough [HDMI 2.1](/glossary/hdmi-2-1/) ports matter if you have multiple consoles.
- **Size.** In a home theater, size matters more than in any other room. The goal is a screen that fills 30 to 40 degrees of your field of view.
- **Processing.** Upscaling, motion handling and accurate picture modes (such as Filmmaker Mode) determine how good everyday content looks.

Built-in speakers barely matter: in a home theater, sound comes from a [receiver and speakers](/best-home-theater-receiver/) or a [soundbar](/best-soundbar-for-home-theater/).

sections.heading: How to Choose the Best TV for Home Theater
sections.body:
Four decisions narrow the field:

1. **How bright is the room?** Dark or dim: OLED (LG C5, Sony Bravia 8 II) gives the best picture. Bright with windows: a bright OLED with an anti-glare finish (Samsung S95F, LG G5) or a Mini LED (Sony Bravia 9, Hisense U8QG).
2. **How far do you sit?** For a 16:9 TV, an immersive 40-degree view means sitting about 1.2 times the diagonal away; a relaxed 30-degree view means about 1.6 times. At 10 feet, that points to 75 to 100 inches. See the size table below or the [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/).
3. **What audio will you use?** For a receiver or soundbar with Dolby Atmos, you need **eARC**. Every pick here has it.
4. **How many HDMI 2.1 devices?** If you have two consoles plus a receiver, a TV with four HDMI 2.1 ports (LG, Samsung) is easier than one with two (Sony).

If the size you want is beyond 100 inches, or you can fully darken the room, read the projector vs TV section below before you buy.

sections.heading: How We Ranked These TVs
sections.body:
We compared every TV in our catalog on:

- **Picture fundamentals:** contrast, HDR brightness, color volume and processing, based on manufacturer specs and widely published independent measurements.
- **Home theater connectivity:** eARC, number of HDMI 2.1 ports, HDR format support.
- **Size range:** how big each model goes, and the price per inch at large sizes.
- **Room fit:** dark-room vs bright-room strengths.
- **Owner-reported reliability**, including panel issues and software support.

We have not bench-tested these TVs in a lab. Rankings come from spec research, published measurements, seat-distance maths and owner reports, and we leave out figures we could not confirm. We deliberately included options for dark rooms, bright rooms, very large screens and tight budgets.

sections.heading: Projector vs TV for a Home Theater
sections.body:
This is the most important decision in a home theater, so here is the comparison in one place.

| Factor | TV (OLED / Mini LED) | Projector |
|---|---|---|
| Size | Mainstream sizes top out around 98 to 100 inches | 100 to 150 inches is routine |
| HDR highlights | 1,000+ nits possible | Typically 100 to 170 nits on screen |
| Black level | OLED: perfect; Mini LED: very good | Depends on projector and room |
| Daytime viewing | Excellent | Needs ALR screen or dark room |
| Setup | Plug in, wall-mount | Screen, mount, throw distance, cabling |
| Cost per square inch at 100 inches and up | High | Low |

**The size maths:** a 120-inch projected image has about **2.4 times the area of a 77-inch TV** and about twice the area of an 85-inch TV. A 100-inch projected image has 2.4 times the area of a 65-inch TV.

**The brightness maths:** a good projector on a 120-inch screen produces around 30 to 50 foot-lamberts, roughly 100 to 170 nits. A Mini LED TV can exceed 1,000 nits in HDR highlights. That is why TVs win on HDR impact and in bright rooms.

**Choose a TV if** you watch in daylight, want the best HDR, or the size you want is 100 inches or less. **Choose a projector if** you want more than 100 inches, can control light in the evening, and want a cinema-like experience. Our [best projector for home theater](/best-projector-for-home-theater/) guide covers the options, and an ultra short throw like the [Hisense PX3-Pro](/gear/hisense-px3-pro/) is the closest projector to a TV experience.

sections.heading: OLED vs Mini LED for Movies
sections.body:
**OLED** (LG C5 and G5, Sony Bravia 8 II, Samsung S95F and S90F) makes light at each pixel. Black is truly black, there is no blooming, and viewing angles are wide, so every seat in the room sees the same picture. The trade-off is brightness: OLEDs are dimmer than Mini LED, especially on full-screen bright scenes, and there is a small long-term risk of burn-in with static content, though modern panels manage this well.

**Mini LED** (Sony Bravia 9, TCL QM8K and QM7K, Hisense U8QG and U75QG) lights an LCD panel from behind with thousands of small LEDs in dimming zones. It gets far brighter, which helps HDR and daytime viewing, and it comes in larger sizes for less money. The trade-off is blooming around bright objects on dark backgrounds and weaker off-angle performance.

**For a dedicated, dark home theater, OLED is the better choice.** For a bright living-room theater, or if you want 85 to 100 inches on a budget, Mini LED makes more sense.

sections.heading: What Size TV for a Home Theater?
sections.body:
Size from your seats. For a 16:9 TV, a 40-degree field of view (THX immersive) means sitting about 1.2 times the diagonal away, and a 30-degree view (SMPTE minimum) about 1.6 times.

| Seating distance | Immersive (40°) | Minimum (30°) |
|---|---|---|
| 6 ft | about 60 in | about 45 in |
| 8 ft | about 80 in | about 60 in |
| 10 ft | about 100 in | about 75 in |
| 12 ft | about 120 in | about 90 in |

Most living rooms put the sofa 8 to 10 feet from the screen, which means **75 inches is the practical minimum** for a home theater feel and **85 to 100 inches** is ideal. With 4K, you can sit at 1.0 to 1.5 times the diagonal without seeing pixels, so "too big" is rarely a problem. At 12 feet or more, only a 100-inch TV or a projector reaches the immersive range. Run your numbers in the [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/).

sections.heading: Connecting a TV to a Home Theater System
sections.body:
There are two main ways to build sound around a TV:

**TV-centric (eARC):** connect your sources (streaming box, console, Blu-ray player) to the TV, then connect the TV's eARC port to a receiver or soundbar. [eARC](/glossary/earc/) carries lossless Dolby TrueHD, DTS-HD and [Dolby Atmos](/glossary/dolby-atmos/). This is the simplest setup and keeps HDMI 2.1 features on the TV.

**Receiver-centric:** connect sources to the receiver, which passes video to the TV. This gives the receiver full control of audio but requires a receiver with [HDMI 2.1](/glossary/hdmi-2-1/) passthrough for 4K/120 gaming. See our [home theater receiver guide](/best-home-theater-receiver/).

A few compatibility notes:

- **Sony Bravia 8 II and Bravia 9** have two HDMI 2.1 ports, one shared with eARC. With two consoles, route one through a receiver.
- **Samsung** TVs do not support Dolby Vision; they use HDR10+.
- **Format passthrough** varies by brand and firmware, so check that your TV passes the audio formats your receiver supports.

For a complete package, see the [best home theater systems](/best-home-theater-systems/) or the [best soundbar for home theater](/best-soundbar-for-home-theater/).

sections.heading: Who Should Buy a TV Instead of a Projector
sections.body:
**Buy a TV if:** your room gets daylight, you want the best possible HDR, you want a simple setup with no screen or mount, or you sit close enough that 75 to 100 inches fills your view. A TV is also the better choice for households where the screen is on all day.

**Buy a projector if:** you want 110 inches or more, you have a basement or dedicated room you can darken, and you are comfortable with a little more setup.

**Consider both:** many home theaters pair a TV for daily viewing with a drop-down screen and projector for movie nights. Our [projector screen guide](/best-projector-screen-for-home-theater/) includes motorized screens that drop in front of a TV.

mistakes.title: Buying too small
mistakes.body: At 9 or 10 feet, a 65-inch TV fills less than 30 degrees of your view, below the home theater minimum. Size up to 75 to 85 inches, or calculate from your seating distance.

mistakes.title: Choosing OLED for a sunny room without checking glare
mistakes.body: Glossy OLEDs reflect windows and lamps. In a bright room, choose an anti-glare OLED like the Samsung S95F or a bright Mini LED instead.

mistakes.title: Ignoring HDMI port limits
mistakes.body: Some TVs have only two HDMI 2.1 ports, and one is often shared with eARC. Count your 4K/120 devices before you buy, or plan to route them through a receiver.

mistakes.title: Relying on TV speakers
mistakes.body: Even premium TV speakers cannot fill a room. Budget for a soundbar or a receiver and speakers, connected via eARC, from the start.

mistakes.title: Leaving the TV in its default picture mode
mistakes.body: Store-demo modes push brightness and blue tones. Switch to Filmmaker Mode or the Cinema preset for accurate movie color, then adjust brightness for your room.

faqs.q: Is a projector better than a TV for a home theater?
faqs.a: A projector is better if you want a picture larger than about 100 inches and can darken the room; a 120-inch image has about twice the area of an 85-inch TV. A TV is better for bright rooms, daytime viewing and HDR, since OLED and Mini LED TVs are far brighter and have deeper blacks.

faqs.q: What is the best TV for a home theater room?
faqs.a: For a dark home theater room, the LG C5 OLED is the best TV for most people thanks to perfect blacks, four HDMI 2.1 ports and Dolby Vision. The Sony Bravia 8 II has the most refined picture for films, and the TCL QM8K is the best value at 85 and 98 inches.

faqs.q: Is OLED or Mini LED better for a home theater?
faqs.a: OLED is better for a dark, dedicated home theater because it delivers perfect black with no blooming and wide viewing angles. Mini LED is better for bright rooms and for very large screens on a budget, because it gets much brighter and costs less per inch at 85 inches and up.

faqs.q: What size TV should I get for a 10 ft viewing distance?
faqs.a: At 10 feet, a 100-inch TV gives an immersive 40-degree field of view, and 75 inches is the 30-degree minimum recommended for home theater. In practice, 85 inches is a great balance of immersion and price, and 4K resolution means you will not see pixels at that distance.

faqs.q: What is the best 85-inch TV for home theater?
faqs.a: The Sony Bravia 9 is the best 85-inch TV for home theater if you want the most refined Mini LED picture. For more value, the TCL QM8K and Hisense U8QG come in 85 inches for considerably less. The LG C5 OLED tops out at 83 inches if you prefer OLED.

faqs.q: Do I need eARC for a home theater?
faqs.a: You need eARC if you send audio from the TV to a receiver or soundbar and want lossless Dolby TrueHD or Dolby Atmos from streaming apps and discs played through the TV. Regular ARC is limited to compressed formats. Every TV in this guide has an eARC port.

faqs.q: Does a TV need Dolby Vision for a home theater?
faqs.a: It is helpful but not essential. Dolby Vision adds scene-by-scene HDR metadata used widely by streaming services and many 4K Blu-rays. LG, Sony, TCL and Hisense support it; Samsung uses HDR10+ instead. Without Dolby Vision, content falls back to standard HDR10.

faqs.q: Is a 100-inch TV worth it over a projector?
faqs.a: A 100-inch TV is worth it if your room is bright or you want simple setup: it stays punchy with lights on and needs no screen or mount. A projector is better value if you can darken the room, because a 120-inch image has about 44% more area than a 100-inch TV.

bottomLine: The best TV for home theater for most rooms is the **LG C5 OLED**: perfect blacks, four HDMI 2.1 ports and sizes up to 83 inches. Film purists should pick the **Sony Bravia 8 II**, while the **LG G5** and **Samsung S95F** are the bright-room OLEDs, the G5 with Dolby Vision and sizes to 97 inches, the S95F with an anti-glare finish. The **Sony Bravia 9** is the most refined Mini LED, the **TCL QM8K** is the big-screen value champion, the **Hisense U8QG** delivers bright-room punch for less, and the **Hisense U75QG** is the budget pick. If you want more than 100 inches and can darken the room, a projector is the better buy.
